Extreme weather

Make room for the days when demand rises and the power plants you counted on cannot deliver.

  • Austin, Texas · 2017

    Deep Freeze

    A grid built for Texas heat is about to face a very different test. You have four years to prepare for the February 2021 freeze.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • San Juan, Puerto Rico · 2000

    Hurricane Season

    A storm can take several power plants out of service at once. Build a Puerto Rico grid with enough room to recover.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Madrid, Spain · 2023

    Heatwave + Drought

    Cooling demand rises just as the water runs low. Hydro produces less, and hot rivers limit nuclear cooling too.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Los Angeles, California · 2022

    Wildfire Emergency

    Most of your spare power comes from somewhere else. In early 2025, wildfire will cut the capacity of your northern connection by 90%.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Lusaka, Zambia · 2012

    The River Runs Dry

    A full reservoir makes the opening years look comfortable. An El Niño drought will test a grid built around the Zambezi.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Delhi, India · 2018

    Delhi Summer

    Every summer needs more cooling. The heat also cuts power plant output, and a late monsoon delays the relief you were counting on.

    Explore scenario ↗

Rapid growth

More customers bring more revenue. They also need power before your next plant is ready.

  • Manassas, Virginia · 2020

    Data Center Boom

    The data centers arrive in 2026. Their power needs are much bigger than your small city utility, and residents still need affordable electricity.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania · 2006

    The Shale Boom

    Cheap gas looks like an opportunity. A power plant is a long commitment to a fuel price that can change much faster.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Burlington, Vermont · 2005

    Across the Valley

    The utility across the valley is for sale. Buying it brings more customers, more equipment and more obligations than the purchase price alone suggests.

    Explore scenario ↗

Energy transition

Replace an aging fleet, cut emissions, and work out what keeps the lights on when the sun goes down.

  • San Francisco, California · 2020

    Carbon Fee

    Coal helped build your company. Now every tonne of emissions comes with a bill, and replacing the old fleet will take time and money.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Honolulu, Hawaii · 2003

    Paradise

    There is plenty of sun and wind. There is also an imported-oil bill, and no neighboring grid to call when local supply falls short.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • San Francisco, California · 2002

    Rise of Renewables

    Clean power is getting cheaper. Demand is growing too. Waiting for a better deal has a cost of its own.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania · 1980

    The End of an Era

    Your company's coal plants are getting old. Their replacements need years to build, and competitors are ready to take the customers you lose.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Paris, France · 2023

    Sudden Nuclear Shutdown

    Your biggest reactor will stop producing power. It will stay offline for the rest of your term. Have something ready to take its place.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Johannesburg, South Africa · 2016

    Load Shedding

    The coal fleet keeps breaking down. Diesel can cover some of the gap, but it cannot make the problem cheap to ignore.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • Kyiv, Ukrainian SSR · 1986

    Chernobyl: Recovery

    March 1986. The disaster is one month away. Your task is to restore electricity service while paying for a damaged reactor that will never produce power again.

    Explore scenario ↗

  • A fictional California utility · 1882

    One small coal plant. One hundred customers. Start a utility in 1882 and leave the next generation a company worth inheriting.
